https://www.thetimes.com/article/conserv.title: We have three months to impress voters, says senior Tory
https://www.thetimes.com/article/conserv.subtitle: Ben Houchen, the Tees Valley mayor, urges Rishi Sunak to set out compelling vision now to win election
https://www.thetimes.com/article/conserv.text:
Rishi Sunak needs to give voters an agenda they can believe in before Christmas if he is to win the next election, says the most senior elected Tory in the north of England.
Lord Houchen of High Leven, who is mayor of the Tees Valley, said that the turnover of prime ministers meant “people are not going to get behind the party that has gone through the last 12 or 15 months” of turmoil and said that Sunak needed to set out an agenda and start to deliver on it before Christmas to win votes.
Speaking at a fringe event at the Conservative Party conference in Manchester, Houchen said that there was a route by which the Conservatives could pull off a victory, and that Sunak had put in the work to calm the political landscape.
But he said: “Where Rishi is now is at a tipping point, that he wants those people to vote for him, we all do, and he’s got the ability to make that happen, but time is running out and over the next, ideally, hopefully this week, he sets out that agenda.
“But certainly before Christmas, he needs to set that agenda out and start to deliver on it, show people that it’s not just words.”
Tory MPs with majorities of less than 8,000 were told that they should start looking for new jobs, and the Conservative Party chairman said that they were heading into the next election as the “underdogs”.
Houchen said Sunak’s priority should be “delivering on the agenda that we were elected in 2019” on. He said this included showing the benefits of Brexit and delivering on levelling up.
He said the coalition of voters Boris Johnson had formed in the so-called red wall, many of whom backed the Tories for the first time, were “really irritated with us” and were thinking “I voted for you for the first time, and now I don’t feel like I can, but now I don’t know what to do”.
Asked if he thought the party could win the next election he said: “Yes, they can. Will they is a different thing.”
But he would not bet on it. “Not at the moment, because we need to do more to give those people that excuse,” he said.
Greg Hands, the party chairman, said the Tories will enter the next general election as the underdogs.
In his speech on the conference’s main stage Hands said: “This is likely to be a general election where the Conservatives enter as the underdogs. I know in recent years you will have had difficult conversations with voters, I certainly have.
“But I would say just three things about those conversations. First, every single conversation I’ve had on the doorstep has been improved by the mention of Rishi Sunak and the job that he does as our prime minister. Second, that there is no enthusiasm for Sir Keir Starmer and even less trust in him.”
Brandishing flip flops with Starmer’s face on to demonstrate Labour’s supposed habit of U-turns, he added, “And third, that wherever Labour runs something in the country, they run it badly.”
Michael Gove, the levelling up secretary, dodged the question over whether the Tories could win.
At a fringe event he said: “I’m not very good at predictions . . . I think showing, not telling, is the answer. We need to demonstrate a record of delivery over the course of the next year.”
Frank Luntz, a pollster, said that Conservative MPs with a majority of less than 8,000 “might want to look for another job”. He told Times Radio: “Some MPs are going to be shocked on election day because the vote against them could be so high.”
Luntz said that he had not picked up massive appetite for a Labour government either. He previously gave a presentation to Tory MPs, telling them that if they had a majority of less than 15,000 they should worry. He said: “I used a 15,000 mark, frankly, to be provocative, and clearly it was. But I would say if your majority is less than 8,000 you might want to look for another job.”
He said that some MPs had heeded the warning and taken steps to appeal to their constituencies directly. “They’re already winning back disaffected Tories,” he said.

Young people are less likely to vote for the Conservatives as they get older because they are being denied the “British dream” of home ownership or parenthood, new research has claimed (Geraldine Scott writes).
Polling by YouGov for Bright Blue, the centre-right think tank, found that 65 per cent of all adults thought making homes cheaper for first time buyers would appeal to young voters.
One Conservative party member in his twenties told The Times: “There is a sense that this government is not prioritising young people and I do worry it will put my peers off voting Tory, even as they age. Specifically like issues on housing, but also taking decisions about HS2 that actually aren’t long-term decisions. But also the triple lock — if they keep that that is showing their priority is pensioners.”
Rishi Sunak said he was focusing on delivering for the British people, not on their perception of him, after he was told some voters associated him with wealth, greed and elitism (Laurence Sleator writes).
In an interview with Laura Kuennsberg on the BBC, the prime minister was shown a “word cloud” showing what people said when asked what they believed he stood for.
The most commonly used word was “rich”, with other prominent ones including “wealth”, “greed”, “upper class”, “elite”, “money” and “himself”. The graphic, conducted by the public opinion researcher More in Common, also included more positive perceptions such as “leadership”, “prosperity” and “fairness”.
In response, Sunak did not directly address the findings and instead talked about his move to push back the sale of new petrol and diesel cars from 2030 to 2035. “My job is to deliver for people ... That was a decision motivated by me wanting to ease the burden on families.”
Britain will deploy 600 peacekeeping soldiers to Kosovo after “concerning” clashes near the border with Serbia (George Grylls writes).
Grant Shapps, the defence secretary, said troops from the 1st Battalion, Princess of Wales’s Royal Regiment would be sent to the nation after a request from Nato to help defuse tensions.
In total, 200 British soldiers will join 400 who are already stationed there. Nato has an overall force of 4,500 troops in the country, with the defensive alliance having first intervened in 1999 with a bombing campaign to prevent the ethnic cleansing of Albanians.
Kosovo, a landlocked country in the Balkans, declared independence from Serbia in 2008. The majority of the population is ethnically Albanian but it has a Serbian minority. Last week, ethnic Serbian gunmen barricaded themselves in a monastery in the country’s north to protest against the Kosovan government. Three of the gunmen died and a Kosovan police office was killed.
Rishi Sunak compared his approach on tax to Margaret Thatcher as he resisted calls to promise a pre-election giveaway.
The prime minister said it was “deeply Conservative” to tackle inflation before cutting tax. “This is what Margaret Thatcher did, this is what Nigel Lawson did,” he said.
“This is in the tradition of great Conservative governments, bringing inflation down, because that’s the bedrock on which you build a strong economy. And that is the best way to help people with the cost of living.”
Despite Sunak’s claims about Thatcher, income tax was slashed in the first Budget of her administration, although VAT was increased.
Earlier Michael Gove called for taxes to be cut before the next election, although he said he would not join Liz Truss and 32 other MPs in refusing to vote for any tax rises.
The Conservative Party chairman just mocked the Labour leader by holding up a pair of flip-flops on the main conference stage.
Greg Hands kicked off proceedings in Manchester by accusing Sir Keir Starmer of being a “man who will literally say anything that suits him at that time”. He said: “Who is the real Sir Keir Starmer? The friend and supporter of Jeremy Corbyn? The puppet of Tony Blair? Or the mouthpiece of Just Stop Oil?”
He then produced a pair of flip-flops with the Labour leader’s face printed on them.
As he showed them off to party members, Hands told the Exchange Hall at Manchester Central Convention Complex: “I always thought that the best leaders wake up each morning, and ask themselves, ‘What am I going to do today?’. Some leaders ask themselves, ‘What am I going to say today?’ Sir Keir wakes up and asks, ‘What am I going to believe today?’
Some observers on social media were quick to point out that Hands was holding the flip-flops the wrong way round, so they read “flop-flip”.
Liz Truss should not be at the Conservative Party conference and should let Rishi Sunak set out his policies without distraction, a leading Tory mayor has said.
Lord Houchen of High Leven, the Tees Valley mayor, said he was “disappointed” that she had decided to attend and make interventions on government policy.
He told an event: “I thought Liz Truss would have more awareness than to, for example, come to Conservative Party conference. I don’t think she should be here.”
Truss is expected to use a speech at a rally at the conference to call for corporation tax to be cut to 19 per cent to drive economic growth. She is expected to argue that high taxes on businesses must not be “normalised” and that the private sector is “drowning in red tape”.
Conservative MPs with a majority of less than 8,000 “might want to look for another job”, a veteran pollster has said.
Frank Luntz told Times Radio: “Some MPs are going to be shocked on election day because the vote against them could be so high.”
The American pollster has given a presentation to Tory MPs telling them to worry for their seats if they have a majority of 15,000 or less. “I used a 15,000 mark, frankly, to be provocative, and clearly it was,” he said. “But I would say if your majority is less than 8,000 you might want to look for another job.”
He said some MPs had heeded the warning and taken steps to appeal to their constituencies directly. “They’re already winning back disaffected Tories,” he said, adding that he did not sense great appetite for a Labour government among voters.
Michael Gove has said he does not need to sign any pledges to show he is committed to lowering taxes.
The levelling-up secretary signalled that he would not join Liz Truss and more than 30 other Tories in vowing not to vote for any autumn statement that contains tax rises.
He said he “completely agreed” that taxes should fall but told Times Radio: “Having been in government for a while, I don’t need to sign any pledges to show my commitment . . . I think that the principle that we should seek to reduce taxation is one that unites the Conservatives.”
Labour is “bomb-proofing” its policies before the general election, Wes Streeting said after the party dropped plans to abolish the charitable status of private schools.
Streeting, the shadow health secretary, said the party was prioritising “what works” and that it was unfair for private schools to be able to claim VAT exemption.
Asked about the charitable status reform, which had been touted by several Labour frontbenchers, he said: “We’re just looking at what would work most effectively and how we can make that difference as quickly as possible.”
He added: “People can take reassurance from the fact that the promises we make in our manifesto at the election will be promises that we can keep . . . We are bomb-proofing every single one of our policies so we don’t end up in the same position as the government.”
Asked whether other policies would be dropped, he said: “It’s no bad thing that we are working really hard to make sure that there is a high bar to get into Labour’s manifesto, and that bar is, ‘Is it credible, can it be delivered, will it make a real difference to people’s lives?’ ”
Suella Braverman may have simply wanted attention when she claimed that multiculturalism in Britain had failed, her predecessor as home secretary has said.
Dame Priti Patel, who was home secretary under Boris Johnson, said integration by ethnic minorities was something to be “proud of” after Braverman said in a speech last week that communities continued to live apart.
Patel told Trevor Phillips on Sky News: “You and I are sitting here today, we are the products of actual integration, multiculturalism, dynamic communities, people who love our country, want to contribute to our country, along with a hell of a lot of other people that have done exactly the same. I think that is something we should be proud of in our country.”
She added: “People want to work and they want to contribute and integrate, so I think context matters a great deal.”
Asked why Braverman made her comments: “I don’t know what the intention was about that, it might just be to get attention, to have a dividing line into a run up to a general election.”
Rishi Sunak refused to be drawn on the future of HS2 but insisted he was “committed to levelling up across this country”.
The prime minister repeatedly said he would not comment on speculation about the high-speed line amid suggestions that the northern leg or other parts of the route may be cut.
Michael Gove, the levelling-up secretary, told Sky News he was a “supporter of strong and good transport links for the north” and thought HS2 was “an important project”. But he said: “We do need to look at value for money and the costs of this project have been significantly greater than originally estimated.”
Sunak rejected the suggestion that scaling back HS2 would make Britain a laughing stock. He said business leaders were “excited about the opportunity that investing in Britain offers”.
• Thirty miles of tunnels, nine minutes of views: what HS2 travel will be like
Councils will still be able to introduce 20mph zones, Rishi Sunak admitted after his promise to curtail their spread.
Tackling “anti-car measures” is expected to be central to the prime minister’s conference speech and will include a clampdown on 20mph limits, bus lanes and low-traffic neighbourhoods in England.
But he confirmed to Laura Kuenssberg on BBC1 that councils remained “in charge of what’s happening in their local areas”.
When Kuenssberg pointed out that several Conservative-led councils were pushing for lower speed limits, he said: “This is about local people being in the driving seat and it’s about making sure that things are not imposed on local communities without their consent . . . It can’t be part of this war on motorists.”
Rishi Sunak has promised to “change how we do politics” and warned that he does not expect everyone to agree with his decisions.
Speaking before his first conference speech as Conservative leader, he said: “You’ve got to take a stand on things . . . People will have a clearer idea of what I believe, what I stand for, and the direction in which I want to leave the country.”
Asked whether he was comfortable with having become prime minister without a mandate from the public or party membership, he said: “I’m doing what I believe is right, I did that last summer, I stood up for my principles. I said what I thought was right for the country.”
Michael Gove has called for tax cuts for working people to be prioritised over scaling back inheritance tax. Gove, the levelling-up secretary, said he wanted to “see the tax burden reduced before the next election”.
Sunak faces pressure from some Tories to increase the threshold at which estates pay inheritance tax as a precursor to abolishing it entirely.
On day one of the Conservative Party conference in Manchester, Gove told Sunday Morning with Trevor Phillips on Sky News: “My own view is that wherever possible we should cut taxes on work. In other words we should incentivise people to work harder, we should make sure that they’re better rewarded for the enterprise, the effort, the endeavour that they put in.”
Dame Priti Patel, the former home secretary, supports the abolition abolish inheritance tax but agreed that voters needed to feel the impact of tax cuts before the next election. “Of course I’d like to see taxes come down, income tax in particular,” she told Sky News. On inheritance tax she added: “I think it needs reforming — quite frankly I’d rather see it go, and I’ve said that many times. It is a regressive and a punitive tax.”
However, Sunak told the BBC: “I’m a Conservative, of course I want to cut taxes. The best tax cut that I can deliver for the British people right now is to halve inflation . . . I believe the country wants change, and we’re going to do things differently to bring about that change.”
Welcome to our live coverage of the Conservative Party conference in Manchester.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/comedy/.title: Sorry for all the jokes, ladies, I’ll get my coat
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/comedy/.text:
Women, revealed a survey this week, aren’t any more attracted to men who make them laugh than they are to those who don’t. So that’s my life’s work up in smoke then. Ever since I can remember, making girls laugh (and then women) has been pretty much my number one mission when I wake up every morning. I don’t need to put “make women laugh” on a to-do list, it’s baked-in. I loved it when I was five years old and I love it still, almost 55 years later.
I make no claim to comedy greatness. And yet, no false modesty, I’ve generated a few chortles down the years. A few female titters, girlish giggles and ladies’ laffs, if you will, not all of them unintentional. Turns out it was a vast conspiracy designed to, literally, humour me. A conspiracy not just hatched by those women on whom I may have had designs but by aunts, cousins, my mother, my daughter … all through those gags, silly walks, mediocre mimicry and, dammit, yes, the occasional genuinely witty bon mot, my desired audience was merely tolerating the whole show, waiting for it to be over. Bummer.
I enjoy making men laugh too, but nowhere near as much as women. Comedy is trickier with men, they can turn resentful, or nasty, or violent. I learnt the hard way that class clown is only ever one ill-timed barb away from becoming the class punchbag. Yet from a very young age, I discovered to my delight that I could reliably make girls laugh, and when they did, there was no sweeter sound. I always assumed generating laughter was part of my appeal, such as it was and is.
In the cold light of this unimpeachable scientific data, however, I am forced to reassess. And when I analyse my romantic relationships, successful and failed, happy and sad, requited and unrequited, the fact is humour wasn’t that significant.
If anything, playing the joker throughout my teens was probably responsible for the wayI was consistently friend-zoned (as youngsters term the dreaded “I like you, but not in that way” letdown) by the subjects of my affection. Romantic success only arrived, funnily enough, when I lost three stone.
Personality plays a huge part in a long relationship but in the context of three-minute speed dating in which the research was conducted, other more obvious factors matter rather more. I think of the judgments I make in similar circumstances and hey, they ain’t especially sophisticated. Why would women be different? Being funny, along with kindness, competence, reliability, etc, may be a welcome bonus should things develop; it is not a first order requirement in kindling sexual attraction.
Then again, these days, sometimes I wonder what it is a young guy is supposed to do to set himself apart from the competition. In my day, you got a tan, lifted a few weights, cracked a joke, bought a drink and that was you, in with a fighting chance. For the generation before that, if old movies are to be believed, it was all about being sharply dressed and having a car. I never quite bought the idea that women fell for a man purely because he had access to an internal combustion engine but if they ever did, they certainly don’t any more. For Just Stop Oil Gen Zedders, turning up in a Jag gets you binned on the spot.
Up until this summer I’d have said maybe soulful guitar-strumming did the trick. But then I saw Barbie where that very ploy was gleefully ripped to bits. And now it turns out wry self-deprecation and delightfully amusing repartee don’t butter any parsnips either. What’s a chap to do?
And yet, as I lurk around the hotspots of east London, I see plenty of young couples, same as it ever was. The guys all look like they’re punching, looks-wise, above their weight: bit weedy; silly beard; scruffy gear. And they damn sure aren’t funny, even if she wanted them to be, which it turns out she doesn’t. So, what has he got? Even though I live close to the City and Shoreditch’s Silicon Roundabout, these hipster chaps can’t all be hedge funders or new media billionaires. I ask again: what have they got? Apart from their youth, of course.
So, farewell “Dodgy” Dave Courtney, showbiz gangster and self-styled loveable rogue, last of the Cockney geezers, hard men with impeccable manners, who’d always be sure to ask after yer muvver as they smashed you in the face with a knuckle duster. Let’s hope all that cheeky villain nonsense dies with dodgy Dave, for all Guy Ritchie’s best efforts to perpetuate the myth.
I spent a fair bit of time with Courtney for an article many years ago. One afternoon, we were hanging out with his mates in his flat in Woolwich, the younger, sillier version of me feeling pretty cool in the company of bona fide criminals. Then Dave announced he had to pop out to “give someone a slap”, which meant hurt them badly. I came to my senses and, in the time-honoured phrase, made my excuses and left. Sensible move.
Many years later, a colleague told me he’d grown up with some of the Adams crime family in Islington. “What were they like?” I asked. “Absolutely horrible,” he replied.
Sitting on the bus to work yesterday morning, Hackney to London Bridge, right through the City, the nation’s capital looked like New York in that post-apocalypse Will Smith film I Am Legend. Well, without the wild animals and prairie grass on Fifth Avenue, but you get the idea. Shops shuttered up, Liverpool Street station semi-deserted, my bus racing along, reaching giddy speeds of, oh, maybe 22mph.
Fridays are quiet anyway and it was half term but even so, the three-day weekend has arrived and shows no signs of going away. I wonder how many of the people who weren’t officially on holiday but didn’t go into the office yesterday could truly say they were working, actually working, from home? For more than a couple of hours? Single figures, I reckon.

Good day, dear Times reader, and welcome to what is technically autumn — but an autumn where until recently people were still wearing shorts and having to take their jackets off as they were “a bit sweaty”.
As anyone raised on Old Moore’s Almanac, or who has any versing in The Olde Ways, will know, men’s knees still being visible two weeks after the autumn equinox is a fundamental disruption to The Way of Things. October is normally the time when everything below the thigh of a man is safely packed away in trousers so that their legs may lie fallow and regenerate during the winter months. I fear that, should “men’s legs” turn into a year-round phenomenon, come spring we may find they have become denuded and spindly, drained of their vital life forces during this unseasonal extra period of skin-showing. We meddle with The Olde Ways at our peril! Although it is too hot for slacks. It’s a true dilemma.
And not the only one! For this week it was announced that the music-streaming platform Spotify is introducing a new tier for subscribers — by which it means, obviously, a new revenue stream for Spotify. The new service — which at $19.99 a month for American subscribers will be roughly twice the standard price — will offer “lossless audio” (whatever that is), AI-generated playlists and at least 20 hours of free audiobook access. Which, to put that into context, is about one third of the Wolf Hall trilogy.
The biggest news, however, isn’t the service that’s being offered but the name it has been given. For Spotify has dubbed this service “Supremium”, a genuinely elevated piece of wordplay. Let us observe how a portmanteau of “supreme” and “premium” transforms the situation, magically upselling the idea of paying twice the standard price for a bunch of things you don’t care about so it seems to become an act of supremacy: you are the winner, perhaps even the god, of Spotify simply because no one else is paying more than you. Not only do you have Supremium, you are Supremium.
And with the invention of Supremium, Spotify has now thrown down the gauntlet to all other tiered service providers to give their most expensive option a similarly swaggering name too. As part of Celebrity Watch’s part-time activities on our Naming Things Bureau, I can obviously offer “UberUber” for Uber’s most uber service, and “PrimeMinister” for Amazon’s prime-best Prime service.
However, when it comes to Twitter/X’s “X Premium” accounts, having coughed up myself and found literally no difference whatsoever — indeed, a notable decline in functionality, reach and service — all I can truthfully offer is “X Premiumly disappointing”.
It’s been a while but this week has the return of Celebrity Watch’s Headline of the Week award — not so much an honour bestowed on, more a panicked survival reaction to, mad things in newspapers.
And the winner is . . . “Daniel Kaluuya’s ‘Barney’ film will ‘not be odd’, says Mattel boss.” This headline works as a series of information bombs seemingly designed to scramble the mind of anyone who was not previously aware that Daniel “Get Out” Kaluuya — one of Britain’s most heavyweight and heavily garlanded actors — was working on a film about Barney, as in Barney the purple dinosaur, the peerlessly goofy/sinister children’s TV, well, dinosaur.
Sure enough, when I googled it, it seems that Kaluuya’s Barney the purple dinosaur film has been in development since 2019 — pre-Covid! — but has not as yet gone into production. One can only presume this hiatus comes from whatever lies behind the Mattel boss’s quote, “will ‘not be odd’ ”. I know we live in an age of miracle and wonder and Barbie explaining patriarchy to loads of Blue Harbour dads, but how can a film about a purple dinosaur not be odd? It’s an unworkable note. Also, if I’m going to see a film about a purple dinosaur, I want it to be odd — to lean away from the oddness would be like trying to make a sequel to Jaws that isn’t too sharky or doing a Star Wars spin-off that’s set in Reading. And where does Kaluuya fit into all this? Is he playing Barney? Obviously his expressive eye work is top-notch, but it would be weird to see this generation’s Robert De Niro peering out from a gigantic purple head.
Still, humans are inventive creatures, so if we can get a man on the moon, we can surely — possibly aided by billions in government funding — de-odd a purple dinosaur. Good luck, everyone!
As someone who prides themselves on being up to date with celebrity news and gossip, I was genuinely shamed this week to learn A Celebrity Fact that has been in the public domain for more than two years. Namely, the actor Kelvin Fletcher, who played the farmer Andy Sugden in Emmerdale for more than 20 years, has left Emmerdale — and become a farmer! He runs a 120-acre livestock farm in the Peak District, which this Christmas will convert into a winter wonderland complete with “giant piano” — nothing more Christmassy than a giant piano! — and Santa meeting “every child in his cosy front room”. There’s no reason why that last sentence should sound slightly menacing, yet it does.
I guess this news has delighted me because I’ve long wondered whether years of playing a character with a specific job leads to actors becoming semi-qualified in the career they depict. I’m pretty sure, after all that time playing a doctor in ER, George Clooney could still reflexively shout, “Cross two units to the head CT, pulse is strong, put in a cervical restraint, let’s intubate!” if he came across someone who’d fallen off a chair. What else is career-specific dialogue in a script if not rote-learning? While wearing a hat? Now that Fletcher has gone from being a pretend farmer to a real farmer, I hope that in coming years we’ll have Danny Dyer opening a pub, Cillian Murphy making an atomic bomb and Meryl Streep becoming prime minister.
Last week, the north was devastated by Rishi Sunak’s announcement that he was cancelling phase two of HS2. Latitudes higher than Watford don’t get transport funding, it seems — the message to the barm cake-eating classes was a firm “put your clogs on and get your steps in”.
This week, however, the north has tried to heal this travel wound with the only medicine left available to it: Liam Gallagher. The Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham announced that the former Oasis frontman will be taking over the passenger announcements on Manchester’s tram network during the Beyond the Music festival, and a spokesperson for Gallagher confirmed that he is “doing his bit”.
● Liam Gallagher review — an electric night of Oasis nostalgia
Thus far, however, what exactly his “bit” consists of has not been revealed. As someone who has decades-long knowledge of Gallagher’s “lively” interview/onstage technique, I feel Manchester should brace itself — in a good way — for some real out-of-the-box stuff: “Keep clear of compilations by the Doors”, “The next stop is NONE OF YOUR BUSINESS”, “MIND THE GAK!”
If the Conservatives really are trying out a whole new live set — as opposed to their official studio releases — it seems they’re part of a trend. For this week social media was set ablaze by reports from disgruntled Pink Floyd fans who’d gone to see the former member Roger Waters play The Dark Side of the Moon Redux at the London Palladium — only for him to spend the first half of the show reading aloud from his autobiography, at present unpublished, instead.
“Rambling nonsense”, “self-indulgent crap”, “a load of old waffle” and “shit” were just some of the harsh-but-fair reviews posted on Twitter from fans who’d paid up to £500 to hear Brain Damage but, by the sounds of it, just got an anecdote about someone called Brian instead.
● Roger Waters review — We don’t need no education on star’s dark side
Still, you can’t argue with Waters’ stagecraft: apparently, when heckled by audience members, he swore at them — then tried to lighten the mood by doing impressions of Bruce Forsyth and Max Bygraves. Max Bygraves! What a pity Waters isn’t still in Pink Floyd — if he were still able to collaborate with David Gilmour, they could have dropped the music entirely and workshopped a whole episode of ChuckleVision together. This is clearly where Waters’ heart is now.
Due to Waters’ unannounced reading from his autobiography — which apparently featured a lot of content about his pets, including a duck called Donald, whom he discussed for 20 minutes — the show overran by an hour. This will have been a crushing blow to his fans, all of whom will have driven into town from Surrey and parked in the big NCP in Brewer Street.
Even at a distance of several days, I can feel the communal agitation of a thousand ageing hippy grandads staring at their Breitlings at 10.02pm and fretting, “That’s another eight quid! On top of my Ulez! I’m being bled dry here!” while Waters wanged on about his duck.
Last week, I was quietly, almost contentedly sure that the Labour Party conference would be incredibly dull. In the lead-up to Keir Starmer’s speech, I certainly wasn’t shouting, “KIDS! It’s starting in five minutes! Who wants to do Doom shots every time they feel a lurch of disappointment in their stomach?” up the stairs in the way I was before Rishi Sunak’s speech at the Tory party conference. In fact, I’d resolved to watch Starmer later on catch-up so I could fast-forward through all the samey bits about “normal, hard-working people”.
Well, more fool me. In the event, Starmer arrived on stage to the carefully chosen Lionheart (Fearless) by Joel Corry and Tom Grennan (uplifting, Italo house piano respectfully nodding to the Tony Blair anthem, D:Ream’s Things Can Only Get Better, but more classy. A big hit across Europe — the seventh most played song in Latvia in 2022! — so a forward-looking choice for re-establishing cross-Channel ties. And if you’re thinking Starmer himself is a “lionheart” and/or “fearless”, well, those are your words, not the words of the playlist compiler). There was clapping. Starmer did some gracious, maybe lionhearted nodding to the audience. He even did that thing where you single out someone in the audience and give them a Special, Happy-Surprised Look, just like Barry Gibb did on the 1998 TV special An Audience with the Bee Gees when he saw Lulu.
And then, of course, Starmer got covered in glitter by a protester. “True democracy is citizen-led! Politics needs an update!” shouted 28-year-old Yaz Ashmawi from the People Demand Democracy group before being wrestled to the ground by a female security guard and led off stage — which was great feminism optics. It took a chick in a ponytail to neutralise a potential assassination threat. Full Mary Earps vibes.
Of course, by that point, wrestling Ashmawi to the ground didn’t really matter — a room full of photographers had already got the shot of Starmer receiving a head full of glitter. Photo after photo showed him in the centre of a Force-like nimbus of spangled glow, while looking 20 per cent perturbed and 80 per cent stoic, like a dad enduring a toddler putting Olaf from Frozen stickers on his nose. Starmer’s jacket came off, his shirt sleeves were rolled up. “If he thinks that bothers me, he doesn’t know me!” he said, seemingly channelling Catherine Tate. The place went bananas. And so, in a blizzard of triumphant vibes and sparkling halos, the speech finally began.
● Keir Starmer speech: key points and policies from Labour Party conference 2023
Of course, the world — and, in particular, Twitter/X — being what it is right now, this incident was immediately fed into a series of conspiracy theory algorithms, and madness starting falling out of the Hot Take Chute. The majority view was that it had all been staged: Labour’s PR department had planned the episode to get that rarest of things, an exciting picture of Keir Starmer — and in a situation that showed him taking his jacket off and popping his cuffs. A bit of alpha wardrobe work.
And, you know, I can entertain that for 30 seconds. People Demand Democracy is a “coalition member” of Just Stop Oil, and that group’s “throwing substance” of choice is usually orange-coloured paint dust. Had Ashmawi top-coated Starmer tangerine, the vibes would have been completely different. Saying “if he thinks that bothers me, he doesn’t know me!” while the colour of Joey Essex just doesn’t land the same way as making a speech while spattered in glitter like Marc Bolan, which plays hard into the 6 Music Dads vote trigger. Since when have protesters coalesced around a glam rock aesthetic?
But ultimately, of course, we know these conspiracy theories are balls: there isn’t some genius, Malcolm McLaren-like figure at Labour HQ going, “What single, throwable substance plays well with Sweet fans, and gay disco fans, and Taylor Swift fans, and small children, and anyone who’s been to Glastonbury? FIND IT AND THROW IT AT KEIR!”
Primarily because, as anyone who has had glitter thrown at them knows, it poses a massive choking hazard — you get a fleck of that on your epiglottis and you’ll be coughing all the way through your greyfield building announcements. However awesome the photo opportunity, it’s not worth the risk of a crucial hour-long speech being punctuated by repeated dry hacking and throat-clearing: humans are fundamentally unreasonable creatures, programmed to deeply hate anyone who coughs more than three times in a minute. In a parallel world where Starmer had gargled the glitter, coughing 270 times in the following 90 minutes, Sunak would win by a landslide in 2024. That’s just who we are.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Jeremy Clarkson: What do we want? A big protest! When do we want it? All the time!
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
It was a big week for the placard industry, because all over the country people were on the streets, chanting and doing protests. Some were supporting Israel. Some were supporting Palestine. And others were demanding free loft insulation for the over-50s.
There was a time when protesters used to sort of take it in turn to make their feelings known. So if you were herding some oxen up Threadneedle Street in the 14th century and you encountered an angry mob of yokels coming the other way, you’d know straight away you’d bumped into Wat Scargill’s revolting peasants who wanted an end to the class system.
And similarly, in 1913, when Emily Davison hurled herself under the King’s horse at the Epsom Derby, no one in the crowd wondered if she was protesting about Australia’s decision to put a kangaroo on its first official stamp. They knew straight away she was a suffragette because, at the time, women’s liberation was the only protest in town.
Even in my living memory, this one-at-a-time mentality was very much the way. For example, in the early 1980s, if you were driving through Berkshire and you stumbled over a bunch of hippie women with hairy armpits and a love of kumbaya folk music, you could be pretty sure they were complaining about the nuclear weapons being stored at Greenham Common.
And then later, if you found a smelly man in a tree, you’d know immediately you’d arrived at a protest about the Newbury bypass. Then, in 1990, if you found a young man with a perm making Jamie Carragher noises as he threw a chair through a shop window, you’d know straight away he was cross about Mrs Thatcher’s poll tax. It was easy back then, but now, when you run into a placard-waving mob, half the time you’ve absolutely no idea what their beef is. Until they appear the following morning on GB News to be shouted at by whatever presenter hasn’t been sacked that week.
It’s reached the point where people from Just Stop Oil can’t get to the Royal Academy to throw soup at a painting because the Tube train they intended to use has people from Extinction Rebellion sitting on top of it. And they can’t borrow their mum’s Volvo either because the roads are blocked by people who are angry about cows.
It’s ridiculous. Secondary school pupils have marched to protest against new rules on how often they can use the lavatory. We’ve had people going berserk outside the Indian high commission to protest about something that may or may not have happened in Canada. And we’ve had people who want to turn back time and rejoin the EU. And that’s before we get to the never-ending stream of people marching to support gay rights and black lives and anti-Nazism.
When there was only one thing worth protesting about at any given time, it could usually get quite a crowd. But what do the weird-beard lefties do now when they decide to spend a day mooching down Oxford Street, in the rain, with a sign? Because every day there’s a smorgasbord of options: “Hey, Humphreyetta, shall we protest about loft insulation or bankers’ bonuses today?” Surely it will get to the point where there simply aren’t enough socialists to go round.
And to make everything even more complicated, every day someone invents a new “issue” on social media or starts a new “conversation” about something that’s been considered normal for four million years. And that’s it. On with the high-visibility jacket. Out with the Day-Glo marker pen. And off we go to shout at a policeman woman and throw a plant pot through a window at HSBC.
All of which brings me on to that Herbert who stormed the stage at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool last week and threw glitter into Sir Starmer’s Playmobil hair. Let’s look first of all at what must have gone through his head. As a committed and enthusiastic protester, he’d woken up and assessed the situation. Hamas had attacked Israel and committed a number of atrocities. Israel had responded with a bombardment that beggared belief. But he decided this wasn’t worth the effort.
Nor was the continuing war in Ukraine or the recent decision to get more oil from the North Sea or Katie Hopkins’s view that women don’t have an inalienable right to have penises. He wasn’t even going to throw in his oar with those who want more Blue Peter dinghies to land on the beaches of Kent. No. He decided he’d make a protest about how there are no “people” in government. “We demand a people’s house,” he yelled. Not sure who the “we” was, but we’ll let that drop.
What are “we” suggesting? That “people” stand as candidates and then other “people” vote for them? Or by “people” does he mean “people” like him? If he does, he’s got a problem. Because it’s hard to serve in a “people’s house” when you are glued to a roundabout in Fulham. Maybe, then, he means “people” like me. Though somehow I doubt that.
I’m sure, however, all will become clear when he appears on what’s left of GB News to explain himself. I’m also sure his protest will wither and die like pretty well every other protest that’s ever been staged. Remember the Countryside Alliance march through London? About 400,000 went on that, to complain about a proposed ban on hunting, and what happened? Hunting was banned.
Then you had the anti-Iraq war march. That was even bigger. Some say a million turned up — and did it work? Well, we went to war with Iraq, so no. Not really. And if a million people can’t change the government’s mind, what chance does a lone Herbert in Liverpool have? And what chance do the loft insulation people have, or the Just Stop Oilers? You can think about that next time you drive down the Newbury bypass, knowing that we still have a class system, protected by a bunch of submarines armed with nuclear weapons.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil protesters spray paint on London’s Wellington Arch
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Three people arrested on suspicion of criminal damage
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Three people have been arrested after Just Stop Oil protesters painted the Wellington Arch in central London orange.
The monument near Hyde Park and Buckingham Palace was sprayed with paint using fire extinguishers. Activists also spray painted the group’s skull symbol at its base.
Three protesters holding banners and flares stood in front of the grade I listed arch, which was built between 1826 and 1830 as an entrance to Buckingham Palace and later became a commemorative arch marking Britain’s victories over Napoleon.
The Metropolitan Police were alerted at about 10.20am, had officers near by and responded quickly, according to Scotland Yard, arresting three people on suspicion of criminal damage.
In recent weeks, the protest group’s actions have included temporarily blocking a coach transporting asylum seekers to the Bibby Stockholm barge and painting university buildings, including in Manchester, Cambridge and Leeds.
The group, which is calling for an end to all new oil and gas projects in the UK, is planning daily marches in London from October 29.
One of the protesters, Joe Hogan, 40, said: “We are out of time. We have to act now ... Traditional, managed, sanitised forms of protest have done nothing. The only way forward is through sustained, disruptive civil resistance.”
On Tuesday three climate protesters were sentenced at Westminster magistrates’ court after being found guilty of aggravated trespass after two ran on to the pitch during the Ashes series at Lord’s and one was prevented from reaching the playing surface after being spotted by stewards.
Judit Murray, 69, Daniel Knorr, 21, and Jacob Bourne, 27, stopped play during the second Test between England and Australia, as security and ground staff cleaned up orange powder that was thrown on the pitch and ensured that the ground was not damaged.
The three had said they wanted to create headlines and did not want to cause disruption or damage the pitch. England player Jonny Bairstow carried Knorr off the pitch, champagne corks and fruit were thrown by cricket fans at Bourne as he was led off the field, and Murray was tackled before she could reach the wicket and held down on the grass, the court heard.
The trio were sentenced to a 12-month community order and 60 hours of unpaid work and will have to pay £330 in costs.
Twelve other Just Stop Oil protesters are in the High Court this week accused of breaching an injunction aimed at restricting protest on the M25 after they caused “considerable delays” in November last year.
