https://www.thetimes.com/article/israel-.title: Hamas releases two sick Israeli women — as it happened
https://www.thetimes.com/article/israel-.subtitle: Yocheved Lifshitz, 85, and Nurit Yitzhak, 80, were driven to the Rafah border crossing
https://www.thetimes.com/article/israel-.text:
Hamas released two more hostages, both Israeli women in their eighties, saying that they were doing so for “humanitarian reasons”.
Yocheved Lifshitz, 85, and Nurit Yitzhak, 79, were driven to the Rafah border crossing between Israel and Egypt, and handed to the Red Cross. They were expected to return to Israel immediately.
The release was negotiated by Egyptian and Qatari officials, though nothing was asked in exchange by Hamas, which hopes to build a degree of international goodwill after the attacks on Israel of October 7.
A statement released by Abu Obaida, nom de guerre of the spokesman of Hamas’s military wing, the al-Qassam Brigades, said: “Through Egyptian-Qatari mediation, we released the two detainees, Nurit Yitzhak and Yocheved Lifshitz, knowing that the enemy has refused since last Friday to accept them. We have decided to release them on humanitarian and health grounds.”
• Israel-Hamas war: released Israeli hostage, 85, describes motorcycle kidnap
It accused the Israelis of committing “violations” of promises to mediators over the course of the day.
Over the weekend Israel dismissed claims it had refused to accept the hostages as “propaganda”.
Rear Admiral Daniel Hagari, spokesman for the Israel defence forces, raised the number of hostages known to be in Hamas’s hands to 222. Scores are known to be dual nationals, including Britons and Americans.
It follows the first release of two American hostages on Friday.
It was unclear whether the women released had other passports. Their husbands are believed to remain in captivity. Both couples lived in Nir Oz kibbutz, near Gaza.
Amiram Cooper, 85, and Yitzhak were pioneers of the kibbutz movement. They last spoke to their family while hiding in the safe room of their house during the attacks. Cooper’s phone signal was later traced to Gaza.
Oded Lifshitz, husband of Yocheved, was said to have volunteered with Palestinian medical students. His wife suffers from Parkinson’s disease and is said to be in regular need of oxygen.
Hamas was earlier reported to be negotiating the release of up to 50 hostages with foreign passports. Israel is said to be reluctant to engage with Hamas’s various demands in response, ranging from a release of Palestinian women in Israeli prisons to an end to the bombing campaign on Gaza.
“We will not refer to false propaganda by Hamas,” a statement from Binyamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, said. “We will continue to act to return the kidnapped and missing.”
The Foreign Office confirmed that, while both women released were Israelis, one of the women has family in Britain.
Lifshitz’s daughter Sharone said: “While I cannot put into words the relief that she is now safe, I will remain focused on securing the release of my father and all those, some 200 innocent people, who remain hostages in Gaza.”
Foreigners should be allowed to assume German citizenship only if they formally pledge to recognise Israel’s right to exist, the leader of the German opposition has demanded (Oliver Moody writes).
Friedrich Merz, leader of the conservative Christian Democratic Union, said there was a risk that the newly naturalised German citizens might be poorly integrated and reject German values such as a commitment to Israel’s security. “Anyone who does not subscribe to this has no place in Germany,” Merz said on German television on Sunday.
• Photos of Israeli hostages held aloft in London
ITV has opened an investigation after claims it interviewed an “Iranian propagandist” who called Hamas’s massacre of Israelis a “homecoming” (Tom Witherow writes).
The Board of Deputies of British Jews accused the channel of a “staggering failure” when it interviewed Latifa Abouchakra in a segment about the spike in Islamophobic abuse in London.
The Palestinian activist and reporter for PressTV, an Iranian state-owned news network, described the massacre of more than 1,400 Israelis as a “homecoming” in a programme broadcast online last week. She added: “At least 1,000 Palestinian fighters from the resistance factions entered the fragile Zionist entity ... over 100 settlers were taken as prisoners of war by the resistance.”
The Board of Deputies wrote in a letter to Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive: “ITV News gave airtime to a literal propagandist for the Iranian regime, a woman who described the mass murder of Jews as a ‘homecoming’. This was a catastrophic breach of your channel’s journalistic standards. I sincerely hope that your channel will be issuing a public apology.”
The news package, which came after the Met Police reported a 140 per cent rise in Islamophobic hate crimes in the capital, was broadcast on ITV London.
ITV News confirmed it is investigating the programme.
Rishi Sunak has declared that chants of “jihad” at protests were a threat to British democracy as plans were drawn up to make sure extremists are arrested at future rallies (David Woode and Matt Dathan write).
The prime minister said that the government would “clarify” guidance given to police after Scotland Yard faced criticism for declining to arrest protesters at a pro-Palestinian demonstration on Saturday.
He insisted that police officers already have the power to arrest those who incite violence or racial hatred and said these should be used to detain people who called for “jihad” against Israel at the rally.
• Read full story here
The White House has sent US military officers with “appropriate experience” to advise Israeli forces ahead of an expected ground invasion of Gaza (Hugh Tomlinson writes).
John Kirby, a White House national security spokesman, said that “a few” US military advisers have been sent to consult with their Israeli counterparts about “their intentions, their strategy, their aims” for the anticipated offensive. But he insisted that the US was “not dictating terms to the Israeli defence force”.
Kirby said that President Biden’s administration was still pushing to secure safe passage for people to leave Gaza, particularly for US citizens, and that negotiations to secure the release of further hostages continued “hour-by-hour”.
Kirby said: “We still want to see safe passage out and particularly for the several hundred American citizens that we know are in Gaza and want to leave.”
He said that securing the first aid convoys into Gaza was “a good start, but it is just a start”.
“We want to see it keep going,” Kirby said. “Whether or not there is a ground invasion, we believe that humanitarian aid flowing to the people of Gaza is critically important, and it needs to go as soon as possible and as much as possible.”
The White House also accused Iran of “actively facilitating” attacks on US bases around the Middle East over recent days and again warned Tehran against using its proxies in the region to escalate the conflict.
A London Underground driver who led pro-Palestinian chants on a train has been suspended (Mario Ledwith writes).
Video footage appeared to show the unnamed driver instigating chants of “free, free Palestine” on Saturday as thousands travelled to a demonstration.
After the footage went viral online, both Transport for London and the British Transport Police launched investigations.
Glynn Barton, TfL’s chief operating officer, said that the driver was identified on Monday and suspended.
Several videos of the incident appeared to show the driver using the train’s announcement system to address passengers.
The driver suggested that he was speaking because of the “hardship and oppression of the ongoing occupation” of the Gaza Strip and West Bank. He chanted “No justice, no peace.”
The Israeli embassy said: “It is deeply troubling to see such intolerance on London’s tubes.”
Close to 10,000 people signed a petition expressing solidarity with the driver’s right to express support for Palestinians.
The Hamas terror attack on southern Israel on October 7 has been seen in footage splashed across the internet — from Hamas’s own live broadcasts from GoPro cameras they strapped to their helmets before the attack, to images relayed by terrified festivalgoers fleeing the automatic gunfire shattering their Supernova “peace party” (Catherine Philp writes).
On Monday the Israeli defence forces invited foreign journalists to a screening too grisly to release. It was a matinee cobbled together with footage from the bodycams of dead Hamas fighters, their dashcams and phones; CCTV from the communities they attacked; video from the phones of Israeli victims and that of emergency responders at each appalling scene.
Such material would, Rear Admiral Daniel Hagari said, form part of “a collective memory for the future” for the Israeli people. It was being screened for the international media but not the Israel press “because they do not need to be persuaded”, he said.
• Read the full story
Ten years ago, I was in the Israeli prime minister’s office in Jerusalem with the man who is so hard to keep out of it, Bibi Netanyahu (William Hague writes). After I had made the longstanding British case for pursuing peace with Palestinians based on two sovereign states, he talked at length about the unreliability of the Palestinian side, bedevilled by weakness, division or extremism. “It is not that a two-state solution is not desirable,” he summed up, “it is that it is not available.”
The assumption that peace is not available can be a dangerous one, because it turns into a belief that it never will be. It then follows that Israel should play off Palestinian factions against each other and undermine their legitimate leadership, as it has done. It means settlers might as well push out more Palestinians in the West Bank. The same view on the other side empowers extremists and means Hamas and Hezbollah will always have recruits for the next war. Each side proves all the more strongly to the other that peace will never be available, nothing more so than the terrorism perpetrated by Hamas two weeks ago.
• Read William Hague’s full column
Humza Yousaf’s family have six bottles of clean water left to share among 100 people and fear they won’t make it through the night, the Scottish first minister has said (Kieran Andrews and Craig Paton write).
Elizabeth El-Nakla and her husband, Maged, the parents of Yousaf’s wife Nadia, travelled to Gaza before the hostilities flared up to visit family earlier this month. They are trapped amid the Israeli airstrikes and border closures.
During a visit to the flood-hit town of Brechin, Angus, on Monday, Yousaf could be seen speaking on the phone and walking away from his advisers to take the call, which was later revealed to be from his mother-in-law.
• Read the full story
A man was arrested after brandishing a knife and shouting Allahu akbar outside a police station in the French city of Reims on Monday (David Chazan writes).
Police tasered him and took him into custody. The man, who has not been named, had been on France’s terror watchlist in the past, but reportedly was taken off it because he was no longer considered a threat.
A police union spokesman said that a “despicable attempted attack” had been foiled.
France raised its terror alert to the highest level after a teacher was stabbed to death 10 days ago by a Russian Muslim extremist who was under surveillance and on the terror watchlist. Days later, a Tunisian who declared himself to be a soldier of Isis murdered two Swedes in Brussels.
Meanwhile, a 37-year-old man was given an eight-month suspended prison sentence for a bomb hoax that forced the authorities to evacuate the Palace of Versailles. The Versailles criminal court ruled that he was mentally impaired and ordered him to seek psychological treatment.
Since the Hamas attacks on Israel, France has suffered a rash of bomb hoaxes that have led to the repeated evacuation of the Louvre museum, airports and other sites. On Sunday, the Palace of Versailles was cleared of visitors and staff for the seventh time in nine days.
Security has been stepped up at at French airports, railway stations and on trains.
A missile fired towards Israel was responsible for the destruction of a hospital in Gaza, Rishi Sunak has said (Geraldine Scott writes).
Citing British intelligence, the prime minister said the bombing of the al-Ahli Arab Hospital was “likely caused by a missile of part of one that was launched from within Gaza towards Israel”.
Speaking in the Commons, Sunak said misreporting on the cause of the destruction had a “negative effect in the region” and that “on the basis of the deep knowledge and analysis of our intelligence and weapons experts, the British government judges that the explosion was likely caused by a missile or part of one that was launched from within Gaza towards Israel.”
Hamas had blamed an Israeli airstrike for the blast. Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador, had also blamed Israel. But the IDF produced audio which it said proved it was the fault of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad militant group.
Sunak, President Biden and other western leaders have issued a joint statement reasserting Israel’s right to defend itself as its attacks on Gaza intensified. The country’s relentless bombing campaign has so far killed more than 5,000 Palestinians, mainly civilians, according to Gaza’s health ministry. • Which countries support Israel — and who backs Hamas?
Sunak has announced that Britain will send a further £20 million of aid to support Palestinians in Gaza (Geraldine Scott writes).
Sunak told the Commons that the Palestinian people are “suffering terribly” and are “also the victims of Hamas who embed themselves in the civilian population”.
He said the government had committed to £10 million of extra support, but there would be another £20 million on top of this.
He said: “Hamas care more about their paymasters in Iran than the children they hide behind.
“There is no scenario where Hamas can be allowed to control Gaza or any part of the Palestinian territories.”
Nineteen activists have been detained by the Dutch authorities for blocking the entrance to the International Criminal Court in the Hague in protest at Israel’s war with Hamas.
Members of Extinction Rebellion took over a bridge in front of the court just after midday, carrying a banner which accused Netanyahu of being a war criminal. Police released all 19.
Originally set up to campaign against climate change, the Dutch wing of the group has staged other pro-Palestinian actions since the attacks by Hamas on October 7.
The demonstration took place as Mark Rutte, the prime minister, arrived in the Middle East to meet with both Netanyahu and the Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas.
The worsening fuel crisis is putting premature babies at serious risk of death, a doctor in Gaza has warned.
The head of the neonatal unit in Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said it will run out of fuel within 48 hours.
Dr Hatem Edhair said there are eight babies in the intensive care unit and ten others in the neonatal department. Half of these children are on CPAP (pressurized air) machines and oxygen machines. If the hospital runs out of fuel, half of these babies will die in less than 24 hours.
Doctors treating premature babies across Gaza have warned that at least 130 are at grave risk across six neonatal units because of worsening fuel shortages. “We are working around the clock,” Edair said. “We need to save these babies.”
Hundreds of ultra-orthodox Jews, who are generally exempt from conscription in Israel, have been voluntarily signing up to serve with the IDF.
The IDF spokesman Daniel Hagari said that the Israeli military had received more than 2,000 requests from Haredi Jews. Some 150 were lining up to enlist today.
According to the Walla news site, the volunteers at the recruitment office in Tel Hashomer are members of the Lithuanian stream of Haredism in Israel aged between 26 and 39.
Haredi women and male yeshiva students are generally exempt from military service. Among non-Haredi Jews, this is sometimes seen as draft dodging.
The Israeli army has said that it thwarted a drone attack that Hamas has claimed responsibility for.
Two UAVs were identified crossing from the Gaza Strip into Israeli territory at Nir Oz and Ein HaBesor near the border, the army said. “Both UAVs were thwarted,” they added, without stating whether they were shot down.
Hamas, which used drones in their October 7 attack on Israel, said on social media that Israeli military posts were the targets of the latest raid.
Israel has said that ground forces have mounted limited raids to fight Palestinian gunmen and that air strikes are being focussed on sites where Hamas was assembling to fight an Israeli invasion.
“During the night there were raids by tank and infantry forces. These raids are raids that kill squads of terrorists who are preparing for our next stage in the war. These are raids that go deep,” Rear Admiral Daniel Hagari said in a televised briefing.
They also used the raids to try to gather information on the 222 hostages being held by Hamas, he said.
Hamas’s armed wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, said that its fighters engaged with an Israeli force that infiltrated Gaza and they destroyed some Israeli military equipment. The group said the incursion by what it described as an armoured force took place east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
“Fighters engaged with the infiltrating force, destroying two bulldozers and a tank and forced the force to withdraw, before they returned safely to base,” a statement said.
There was no Israeli comment about the destruction of equipment.
• Why are Israel and Gaza at war? The history of the conflict explained
The Speaker of the National Assembly in France has accused Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the hard-left leader, of “putting a target on her back” by claiming that she visited Israel “to encourage the massacre” (David Chazan writes).
Yaël Braun-Pivet, who is Jewish, says that she has been repeatedly targeted by antisemitic insults and threats since becoming the first female Speaker of the National Assembly last year.
Mélenchon tweeted that she had been “camping in Tel-Aviv to encourage the massacre”.
Braun-Pivet told France-Inter radio that she believed he had chosen the word “camping” because of its associations with Nazi concentration camps.
Mélenchon dismissed the allegation. “This absurd policing of words is a pitiful diversion to redirect attention from her serious political error,” he tweeted.
Braun-Pivet, a member of President Macron’s centrist governing party, responded: “I never said that I unconditionally support the government of Israel but I unconditionally support the existence of Israel.” She reiterated French support for a two-state solution.
She visited Kibbutz Beeri, which was attacked by Hamas gunmen on October 7, and the site of a music festival where hundreds of people were killed.
Mélenchon, the leader of the France Unbowed party, has refused to describe Hamas as a terrorist group. This has provoked a crisis in his left-wing parliamentary alliance, Nupes, which also includes Greens, centre-left socialists and communists.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 5,087 people in Gaza since the war started on October 7, Hamas officials have said.
Some 2,055 children and 1,119 women are among the dead, while 15,273 people have been injured in the bombardments, the Hamas-run health ministry in the Gaza Strip added.
The ministry put the death toll in the past 24 hours at 436, including 182 children. It said that most of the fatalities had occurred in the southern Gaza Strip, where Israel’s military has ordered Palestinians to evacuate to. The claims have not been independently verified.
Israel is putting up tent cities to rehome some of the tens of thousands of citizens evacuated since the war broke out.
Amir Gissin, the CEO of Maccabi World Union, told Israeli television that Kfar Maccabiah will provide temporary homes for 1,000 people.
He said that the numbers would be limited in order to ensure that everyone there can safely reach a bomb shelter during sirens in the Tel Aviv suburb.
The Red Sea resort of Eilat is also planning on setting up a tent city to accommodate those who have had to flee their homes.
Four teenagers have been arrested in France and Belgium for allegedly planning a terror attack on the Israeli embassy in Brussels (Adam Sage writes).
The arrests occurred this summer before the latest outbreak of violence in the Middle East but were only disclosed this weekend.
Amongst the suspects are two boys, one aged 15 and French, the other 16 and from the mainly Muslim Russian republic of Chechnya. They both went to a school in Tours in the Loire Valley where, according to police sources, they proclaimed their allegiance to Islamic State.
The French adolescent obtained excellent marks for his schoolwork but was regularly punished for inciting classmates to “kill infidels”, police sources say.
A police inquiry was launched this spring when the two adolescents were discovered hidden behind a bush in a public park showing four friends how to make explosives. Police were called after passers-by heard an explosion.
Police found that the two teenagers were in contact with other Islamist radicals, notably a 16-year-old Belgian and a 16-year-old from the Russian Caucasian republic of Ingushetia. Both have also been arrested.
They also discovered that they had created a group entitled Plan d’Assaut on Olvid, the messaging platform. In one message the French teenager laid out plans to attack the embassy, according to Le Parisien newspaper. “Don’t forget that our goal is to terrorise them,” he wrote. “There must be as much blood as possible.”
Lawyers for the suspects described them as “young and vulnerable” and said they had been “manipulated” by Islamist radicals.
European Union leaders will back a United Nations call for a ceasefire to act as a “humanitarian pause” in the Israeli-Hamas conflict at a Brussels summit this week (Bruno Waterfield writes).
A confidential draft diplomatic text, for a meeting of the European Council on Thursday, seeks to woo Arab countries such as Egypt that the EU is trying to negotiate migration deals with.
“The European Council supports the call of [UN secretary general] Guterres for a humanitarian pause in order to allow for safe humanitarian access and aid to reach those in need,” the draft, seen by The Times, says.
EU leaders are divided on how strong expressions of support for Israel should be. The EU fears that its support for Israel is alienating Arab and African neighbours at a time when European governments are trying to build closer links to stop migration flows across the Mediterranean with Tunisia, Egypt and Libya.
The draft text says: “[The EU] reiterates the need for the immediate release of all hostages without any precondition.” The document text also says that the Palestinian Authority should be included in talks and backs a two-state solution.
Germany is uneasy with the calls for a truce as EU foreign ministers discuss the ceasefire call at a meeting in Luxembourg today. “We cannot contain the humanitarian catastrophe if Gaza’s terrorism continues. There will be no security and no peace for either Israel or the Palestinians if this terrorism continues,” Annalena Baerbock, the German foreign minister, said.
A third aid convoy has entered the Gaza Strip from Egypt today (Joshua Thurston writes).
More than a dozen lorries crossed the border at Rafah, according to AFP, adding to a previous total of 34 lorries that had entered Gaza, according to an Egyptian Red Cross official.
Deliveries of aid began on Saturday after shelling on the Gaza side of the border and quarrelling over procedures for inspecting the aid packages left relief materials stranded in Egypt.
At least 100 lorries a day are needed to provide the basic needs of Gaza’s 2.4 million inhabitants, the United Nations has said.
Foreigners should only be allowed to assume German citizenship if they formally pledge to recognise Israel’s right to exist, the leader of the German opposition has demanded (Oliver Moody writes).
The coalition government under Olaf Scholz, the chancellor, has made it possible for people from other countries to obtain German nationality in as little as five years if they can demonstrate that they have lived in the country for at least that time and have a reasonable command of the language.
However, Friedrich Merz, leader of the conservative Christian Democratic Union, said there was a risk that the newly naturalised German citizens might be poorly integrated and reject basic German values such as a commitment to Israel’s security.
“Anyone who does not subscribe to this has no place in Germany,” Merz told German television on Sunday night.
Politicians from across the spectrum of the German right have previously argued that the country has a problem with “imported” antisemitic and anti-Israeli attitudes among migrants from the Islamic world.
Hamas has claimed that its fighters have engaged with Israeli forces in the Gaza Strip and destroyed some Israeli military equipment (Joshua Thurston writes).
The group’s armed wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, said that fighters engaged with the force east of Khan Younis in the south of Gaza, causing the Israelis to withdraw.
The Hamas fighters claim to have destroyed two bulldozers and a tank before returning safely to base.
There was no immediate Israeli comment about the destruction of Israeli equipment or vehicles, however the IDF said yesterday that one soldier was killed and three others were wounded during a tank operation inside Gaza.
In the Israeli-occupied West Bank, two Palestinians were shot dead during an Israeli army raid on the Jalazone refugee camp, the Palestinian health ministry has said (Joshua Thurston writes).
Residents of the camp near Ramallah told Reuters that Israeli forces raided the camp, carried out arrests and clashed with gunmen and youths throwing stones.
About 20 people were arrested, according to the health ministry.
The Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that at least 120 Palestinians were arrested across the West Bank overnight, including 59 in the city of Hebron. Residents said that Israeli forces had retreated to the camp’s outskirts.
Tensions are high in the West Bank. At least 90 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, largely during violent protests and gunbattles during military arrest raids
The Israeli army has not issued a statement about the incident.
President Macron is to visit Israel on Tuesday and is also expected to visit Cairo in an attempt to secure the release of hostages held by Hamas (David Chazan writes).
One French citizen is known to be among some 222 people abducted and six other French nationals have been missing since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October. Hamas released two American hostages last week after Joe Biden visited Israel.
The number of hostages being held in Gaza is now believed to be 222, according to the IDF (Josh Thurston writes).
The Israeli army spokesman Daniel Hagari said that the military had so far notified the families of 222 hostages held by Hamas in Gaza since 7 October. Hagari said a significant number of the hostages were foreign citizens.
The number does not include Judith Raanan and her daughter Natalie, who were released by Hamas on Friday.
When asked whether the ground invasion was being delayed to allow for attempts to secure the release of further hostages, Hagari said: “We are working in all ways to free the hostages and bring them home.”
A British woman whose elderly parents are missing in Gaza has called for a medical corridor to be established for hostages being held in the territory.
Sharone Lifschitz from London said that she had not heard from her mother and father, both in their 80s and with complex health needs, since they were abducted from their home on October 7.
They are among the rumoured 212 hostages believed to be in Gaza.
Speaking on Times Radio, Ms Lifschitz said: “There is a humanitarian corridor which is going into Gaza but we don’t have a medical corridor to the hostages.
“My father had high blood pressure the night before [he was taken] – can I please know if a doctor saw him? I think that everybody has the right to have their family looked after and to have minimal care.”
Asked whether she thinks Binyamin Netanyahu is doing enough to help the hostages, Ms Lifschitz said “Well, do you?”, before adding: “He is the one having my parents’ lives in his hands.”
The White House promised to secure the “continued flow” of aid into Gaza after a call between President Biden and Binyamin Netanyahu, following the arrival of a second aid convoy through the Rafah crossing (Catherine Philp writes).
Biden has urged Israel not to begin any ground offensive until a sustained flow of aid is established and until further negotiations over the release of 212 remaining hostages.
A White House summary of the call said Biden and Netanyahu has agreed that “there will now be continued flow of … critical assistance into Gaza.”
However, the United Nations warned that the volume of aid entering Gaza was just 4 per cent of the daily average required before the war and a fraction of what was needed under the “total blockade” imposed by Israel. Food, water, medicines and fuel stocks are close to running out in Gaza, Israel has refused to allow fuel into the territory despite it being needed to keep hospital generators running, because of fears it could be diverted for use by Hamas vehicles or as a propellant in weapons such as rockets fired at Israel.
The World Health Organisation has said that it is “almost impossible” for hospitals to comply with an Israeli demand to evacuate Gaza’s north and has called on Israel to reconsider the order (Josh Thurston writes).
“There are patients who are there that cannot simply be moved, many there are on mechanical ventilators, there are newborns on incubators, people in unstable conditions, and it’s very difficult to move them,” the WHO spokesman Tarik Jasarevic told the BBC.
Jasarevic said the four trucks of surgical and trauma materials brought into Gaza recently through the Rafah border crossing were “not nearly enough”.
More trucks loaded with supplies were ready to go on the Egyptian side of the border, but more security guarantees were needed, added Jasarevic.
Police will be told to use the “full force of the law” against pro-Palestine protestors, after the Metropolitan Police said that no offence had been identified in a video showing a man shouting “jihad” (Geraldine Scott writes).
Mark Harper, the transport secretary, said that Suella Braverman would make it clear in a meeting today with Sir Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, that she expects the police to act.
Harper told Times Radio: “I saw those clips of that chanting at the weekend. I along with many people would have been very disturbed by it.” He added: “The government feels that the police should use the full force of the law.”
Britain should not be considering taking refugees from Gaza, the transport secretary has said. Mark Harper told Sky News that “reaching for the tool of refugees at this stage is not the right one to do”.
He said: “I think the most important thing is to support people in the region and that’s why we’ve been urging the Israeli government and the Egyptian government to make sure that aid can get into Gaza.
“We saw the first stages of that at the weekend, and that was very welcome, and we will continue to urge that and we will continue to put our support into helping people on the ground.”
The Israeli education ministry has said that it will remove any reference to the climate activist Greta Thunberg after she published a post on Friday supporting Palestine and calling for a ceasefire (Josh Thurston writes).
“This stance disqualifies her from being an educational and moral role model, and she is no longer eligible to serve as an inspiration and educator for Israeli students,” the ministry said.
More than 100 Israeli environmental leaders and activists signed a letter to the young climate activist after she posted on X/Twitter, saying: “Today we strike in solidarity with Palestine and Gaza. The world needs to speak up and call for an immediate ceasefire, justice and freedom for Palestinians and all civilians affected.”
Thunberg later clarified: “It goes without saying — or so I thought — that I’m against the horrific attacks by Hamas.”
Rishi Sunak, President Biden and other western leaders have issued a joint statement reasserting Israel’s right to defend itself as its attacks on Gaza intensified.
After a meeting with Binyamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, Biden spoke to the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany and Italy, the White House said.
A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “The leaders reiterated their support for Israel and its right to defend itself against terrorism and called for adherence to international humanitarian law, including the protection of civilians.”
The leaders also agreed to continue close diplomatic co-ordination, including with key partners in the region, to “prevent the conflict from spreading, preserve stability in the Middle East, and work toward a political solution and durable peace.”
The Israel defence forces said about 320 targets belonging to the Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad terror groups were struck in the Gaza Strip over the past day. Airstrikes also hit targets across the territory early on Monday, including in areas where Palestinian civilians have been told to seek refuge.
• A second convoy of 14 aid trucks entered the Rafah crossing to the besieged Gaza Strip on Sunday night.
• Israel bombarded Gaza and southern Lebanon overnight with airstrikes.
• Binyamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, convened a meeting on Monday morning of his top generals and his war cabinet to assess the escalating conflict.
• President Biden and European leaders issued a joint statement on Sunday night supporting Israel, but also urging it to protect civilians in Gaza.
• Health authorities in Gaza said at least 4,600 people had been killed in Israel’s two-week barrage that began after a Hamas terror attack on Israel on October 7 in which 1,400 people were killed and 212 were taken hostage.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil allowed to recruit at Oxford University freshers’ fair
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Oxford University’s student union has allowed Just Stop Oil to potentially recruit new members by hosting a table at its freshers’ fair.
The climate change protest group manned a small stall at the two-day event this week alongside a number of talks aimed at bolstering its membership.
Members of the group, which routinely targets public events to attract attention, have long regarded universities as key recruitment grounds.
The group is holding a series of “student welcome talks” in Oxford over coming weeks, including one with Roger Hallam, the co-founder of Extinction Rebellion and now a leader in Just Stop Oil.
This is part of a wider six-week push at universities across the country aimed at recruiting enough new members to “overwhelm” police at street protests in coming weeks.
Last month, Gillian Keegan, the education secretary, wrote to vice-chancellors encouraging them to ensure students were “aware of the consequences” of engaging in illegal protest. She said they should be aware of a “heightened risk of unlawful activity” on campuses.
The group’s small stall at the Oxford Student Union this week was manned by Daniel Knorr, a 21-year-old biochemistry student who has attracted media attention for his stunts. The activist was carried off the pitch at Lord’s by the England cricketer Jonny Bairstow in June after he and two other protestors ran on to the pitch during the second Ashes Test.
The student also posted 17,000 leaflets to students via their college cubby holes this week, the Daily Mail reported.
Knorr told the Daily Mail: “We are asking fellow students to take part in nonviolent civil resistance. Young people will live to experience the worst effects of climate breakdown.
“I hope Oxford University continues to enable freedom of thought and assembly to its students.”
The union vets students who apply to host a stall at the freshers’ event for a small fee. A spokesman for the union said: “The last two days have seen over 10,000 students attend the Oxford SU freshers’ fair.
“Oxford SU is a proud supporter of free speech and as such would never deny any student society the opportunity to have a stall at our freshers’ fair on a first come first serve basis.’
Oxford University said that it supported freedom of speech but not illegal protest. A spokesman said: “Oxford University supports the right of all our students and student groups to express views of all persuasions within the law.
“The university does not support illegal action, including any unlawful protesting, and may, within its powers, take any steps it considers appropriate against any student guilty of such behaviour.”
Leaked emails recently revealed how the climate group, which wants the government to stop issuing new fossil fuel licenses, is actively courting student members for new protest actions.
After a slump in its attention-seeking protests in recent weeks, the group is gearing up for a so-called slow march through London later this month on what it says will be an “unprecedented scale”.
The emails suggest that the group plans for 3,000 protesters to be arrested during the action, of which it would like about 500 to be students. The “strategy for student mobilisation” plan stated that this number of arrests would overwhelm police stations and the courts, forcing the government to address its demands.
It further outlined how the group would launch a “massive push” around fresher’s week through talks and potentially carrying out disruptive actions. This is to be followed, the leak stated, by a “dynamite turbo boost” of actions around campus, including spray-painting university buildings with fake oil.
Welcome talks have been lined up by the group at universities in Exeter, Birmingham, Plymouth, Lewisham, Bristol and York over the coming weeks.
Oxford students have previously taken part in Just Stop Oil stunts. The university’s earth sciences department hosted activist Phoebe Plummer, who made headlines for throwing soup at a Van Gogh painting, for a talk in May.
Oxford’s new vice-chancellor, Professor Irene Tracey, declared climate change “the greatest challenge of our time” in an oration earlier this week.
On Wednesday, five Just Stop Oil activists were arrested after they disrupted a performance of Les Misérables in the West End of London. Four young protesters were loudly booed after they invaded the stage at the Sondheim Theatre then unveiled large orange banners and shouted campaign slogans. The cast tried to continue before the music stopped and they were rushed backstage.
The activists stood shouting “Just Stop Oil”, but were quickly drowned out by angry audience members, who whistled, booed and heckled them, yelling: “Get off, you stupid people,” and “How dare you!”
As the curtain came down the protesters locked themselves to the set, prompting the theatre to be evacuated.
• Five people have been charged with aggravated trespass after Just Stop Oil protesters disrupted a performance of Les Misérables in London’s West End.
On Thursday night, the Metropolitan Police identified Hannah Taylor, 23, Lydia Gribbin, 28, Hanan Ameur, 22, Noah Crane, 18, and Poppy Bliss, 19, as the activists involved in the stunt. The group was videoed storming the Sondheim Theatre’s stage on Wednesday.
The five activists have been bailed to appear at Westminster magistrates’ court on November 3.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/middle-ea.title: Pro-Palestinian activists: We’ll target UK defence and council sites
https://www.thetimes.com/world/middle-ea.text:
Pro-Palestinian activists are plotting attacks on defence manufacturers in Britain and the occupation of seats of local government that backed Israel following the massacres by Hamas.
Members of Palestine Action spoke about smashing up buildings with sledgehammers during a 90-minute online “workshop” for the militant group on Wednesday evening.
They are seeking ways to target the defence electronics firm Elbit Systems UK, a subsidiary of the Israeli company Elbit Systems, which has a number of British sites.
An activist also supported a proposal to occupy Bristol’s city hall after it was lit up in blue and white in support of Israel, saying: “I love it, let’s do it.”
Drew Robson, one of the group’s members, told the meeting: “I don’t know if any of you went to the marches — they were amazing, they were great, but it can’t just end there.
“We need to keep hold of that pain, and that anger, and say: ‘I’m going to do something with this and I’m going to make a dent here,’ because we really can make a difference. We just need people to step up with us.”
The group was founded in 2020 by Huda Ammori, an ex-campaign officer for the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, and Richard Barnard, a former Extinction Rebellion activist.
It has repeatedly used civil disobedience tactics to target Elbit, including temporarily shutting down a Leicester drone factory on Wednesday by driving a van at a gate. Three people were arrested at the UAV Tactical Systems factory, a subsidiary of Elbit.
Hours later, Robson appeared on screen at the virtual workshop, held over Zoom, with a second Palestine Action member, Joe, a musician and teacher who works in the public sector. The pair proceeded to show the 39 people who attended an hour-long Powerpoint presentation entitled “100+ years of British Complicity”.
They explained that everything the group did was about “disruption”. As well as Elbit Systems UK, they named two other defence and technology companies to target in Britain, Rafael and Teledyne.
The pair spoke about how members of Palestine Action smash up buildings, spray paint, let off flares, pour expanding foam down gutters and lock themselves to equipment.
Robson said: “It’s an umbrella of activities. We’ve got people going in with the sledgehammers and quite literally taking the place to bits. We’ve got locals outside doing vigils once a week and we’ve got people petitioning the local councillors.”
Joe said: “There are also people who go to arms factories at night, or in secret, and they’ll smash the windows or they spray paint on the windows or they do something to disrupt.
“I haven’t done any of those actions but I really approve of them.”
Participants were urged to download the encrypted message app Signal to communicate, and new recruits were warned “never” to talk to the police and to give a “no comment” interview if arrested.
• What could the Israel-Hamas war mean for the UK?
Defending breaking the law, Joe said: “You’ve committed an offence in order to prevent a greater crime being committed in Palestine.”
One member of the public at the meeting suggested occupying Bristol City Hall because it “lit up in blue and white showing the Israeli flag a few days ago”. Robson said: “Yeah I love it, let’s do it. I like it. If you’re up for kind of having a chat about that, then I’m game for having a chat with you about it.” Joe responded: “That sounds brilliant.”
Indicating that it was poised for imminent action, the group said it would be in touch with those interested in joining “quickly”.
Palestine Action said on Thursday night that the purpose of its workshop was “to inform people of British complicity with apartheid Israel” and alert them to its different “campaigning methods”.
It claimed that “channelling anger into campaigning” was a “constructive way” to help the Palestinian people.
Palestine Action said that Bristol city hall was not a focus of its campaign but added: “By lighting up their building in Israel colours, they are actively endorsing an apartheid state and manufacturing consent for Israel to commit the ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.”
• Why are Israel and Gaza at war? The conflict explained
A spokesman for Elbit Systems UK said: “We take the welfare of our employees extremely seriously and as well as taking our own security measures, we work with the police and authorities to take action against any person or group who sets out to cause them harm.”
Ministers will push ahead with a ban on public bodies boycotting Israel next week as the government moves to solidify its support for the country. The Economic Activity of Public Bodies (Overseas Matters) Bill is due to reach the report stage in the House of Commons on Wednesday, allowing MPs to debate the subject. The timing risks inflaming tensions as the conflict continues.
It is understood that the push to advance the bill came from No 10 after consistent backing from Michael Gove, the communities secretary.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Corporate money for the arts? Bring it on
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
Crisp morning, blue sky and brilliant sun outside the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris. Built by that starriest of starchitects Frank Gehry, the foundation is looking its flashiest, trashiest best. This isnât a discreet museum tucked away in a maison particulier. This is a gleaming Dubai-sur-Seine, a temple to art paid for by champagne, perfume and luxurious small leather goods. Magnifique.
If thereâs a part of me that wrinkles my nose at the giant LV logo above the door, where in a more traditional museum you might have a frieze to the glory of the muses, it is handbagged into submission by the part of me that wants to clap Bernard Arnault â managing director of Louis Vuitton MoÃ«t Hennessy and the second-richest man on earth â on the shoulder and say: âChapeau, mon braveâ.
We are too squeamish about corporate sponsorship of the arts. There is a noisy contingent who pout, petition and protest against nasty, dirty businessmen funding museums, galleries, opera houses and literary festivals. Itâs the Extinction Rebellion (XR) eco-occupiers who lay siege to the British Museum over its links to BP. Itâs the signatories who berate Sadlerâs Wells for its partnership with Barclays, financer of fossil fuel extraction. Itâs the authors who demand that the Edinburgh literary festival cut links with Baillie Gifford, an investment company that invests 2 per cent of its clientsâ money in firms with an interest in fossil fuels.
â¢ Edinburgh Festival leaps to defence of sponsor over âgreenwashingâ
As one must always say at this juncture, I am not a climate change denier. Iâm anti-plastic and pro-vest. Iâm a zero-waste zealot but a net zero sceptic. Weâre going to need fossil fuels for some time yet. So I support the protestersâ concerns but not their means or their timeline. I have a hunch that what XR really hates is less the spoliation of the planet, more big business, men in suits, the City and all its works â the usual cufflinked villains loathed by left-leaning students and unemployed graduates.
This leaves museums and galleries in a bind. The same angry young men and women who deplore BP, Baillie Gifford and Barclays also hate the idea of charging for entry. A reminder: cost of an adult ticket to the Louvre, â¬17; cost of an adult ticket to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, $30; entry for an adult to the British Museum, free as the wind â if the wind were heavily subsidised, sponsored and topped up with sales from novelty Rosetta Stone rubbers.
Corporate money â out. Ticket revenue â out. That leaves money from government, which to the bucket hat-wearing rebels is in every other context the wicked witch but in the context of arts funding becomes the good fairy.
Itâs a delusion, though, that grants are automatically good or that funding comes without ties. Talk to the directors and finance officers at small galleries and they will tell you of form-filling and hoop-jumping and 100-page submissions (see: supporting documents) with no guarantee of the requisite cheque. At a time of budget cuts, the effort invested becomes ever more of a gamble. It takes clever, passionate, creative curators away from the business of putting on exhibitions, caring for collections and running a top-notch half-term activity week for children and their parents. As it happens, Arts Council England has proved itself very far from a good fairy when it comes to its capricious, ill-thought-through treatment of English National Opera. Cuts, demands for a relocation, continuing uncertainty about future support â Iâd rather take my chances with the money men.
â¢ Greta Thunberg pulls out of Edinburgh book festival over sponsor
The aversion to business greasing the arts is deep-rooted. Walking past the Frieze art fair tents last week I saw a sign to the Deutsche Bank lounge and, yes, there went my nose, wrinkling away. Deep-rooted â but that doesnât mean it canât be rooted out. We need a complete mental shift so that when you see âThe Credit Suisse Exhibition: Frans Halsâ outside the National Gallery or âHyundai Commission: El Anatsuiâ on the wall of Tate Modernâs Turbine Hall, you donât say: âSound the Mammon klaxon!â You say: âGood old Hyundai! Three cheers for Credit Suisse! And how about another million sterling next year?â
If it means tax breaks and knighthoods, why not? We give peerages for donations to political parties. At this point in our electoral cycle Iâd rather the money went to Turner Contemporary than the Conservatives. Letâs have, Ã  la Louis Vuitton, a Mulberry Museum and an Anya Hindmarch Gallery of Applied Arts. There are risks, of course. Problematic, those Sackler galleries. And as for Henry Tate . . .


But not all profit is evil, whatever the placards might say. You may also correctly point out â putting Arnault and his deep philanthropic pockets aside for a moment â that French government funding of the arts is generous. It is. But, I would argue, having lived in Paris and done practically a gallery a day for a year, that French galleries are at best laissez-faire and at worst lazy when it comes to the money-spinning side of things. No cafÃ©, no shop (or a paltry cafÃ© and a creased postcard shop) and no nice, big room to hire for a wedding. That goes for the big tourist-pulling chateaux and gardens as much as for the artistâs house in a sleepy commune. Handouts foster dependence. Tight purse-strings make small British galleries nimble. But youâve got to sell a lot of flat whites before you can pay the insurance bill on a world-class collection.
We need a much better, brasher, more boastful culture of arts philanthropy in the UK. And if that means a Burberry concession in the British Museum, well, Iâll take a keyring.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil vandalises Oxford University landmark with paint
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Two protesters used fire extinguishers to cover the walls of the Radcliffe Camera building
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil vandalised an 18th-century building at Oxford University, spraying the Radcliffe Camera in orange paint.
At about midday on Tuesday two students, one of whom claimed to study at the university, used a fire extinguisher to deface the front entrance of the building.
The circular Radcliffe Camera building, which houses the History Faculty Library, links the Bodleian Old Library by the underground Gladstone Link.
Named after the physician John Radcliffe, the building is one of the most recognisable views in Oxford and its architecture was said to have influenced CS Lewis in his work.
Daniel Knorr, a 21-year-old biochemistry student at Oxford, and Noah Crane, 18, a recent A-level graduate, claimed responsibility for the vandalism.
A video showed two police officers forcibly removing one of the students. In another video an officer is seen holding the protesters’ hand as he sits on the grass outside the building.
Knorr said: “I am taking action to resist the destruction of my generation.
“Oxford academics are fully aware of the scale of the climate crisis: this year Oxford scientists said that in a few years climate breakdown will routinely expose people to unsurvivable heat and humidity.
“In other words, hundreds of millions of people will be forced to move, or die. This is mass murder. It is genocide.”
He also called for a commitment by the university to issue a public statement calling on the government to end new fossil fuel licences.
This was not the only action taken by students supporting Just Stop Oil on Tuesday.
George Simonson, 23, a mechanical engineering graduate from the University of Edinburgh, used buckets of paint and spray cans to paint the glass façade of The Forum on Exeter University’s campus.
The graduate unfurled a Just Stop Oil banner and also sat on top of the roof to the entrance of the building, prompting a small crowd to form below him.
A statement from Thames Valley police said: “At around 12.25pm today we received reports of criminal damage on Radcliffe Square.
“Officers attended the scene and are investigating the incident.
“A 21-year-old man from Oxford and a 18-year-old man from Norwich have been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage. They remain in police custody at this time.”
Devon and Cornwall police have also been contacted for comment.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/squire-.title: Squire Steve Coogan doesn’t hate the royals. It’s the flag-waving little people he can’t abide
https://www.thetimes.com/article/squire-.text:
I don’t think it will come as a big surprise that our premier Jimmy Savile cosplayer, Steve Coogan, is, unlike Savile, not a huge fan of the royals. On a food podcast last week he described himself as an “anti-monarchist”: while he liked the Queen (“worked very hard”, “all right”) and didn’t mind “Duchy of Cornwall produce”, generally he felt “the rest are problematic”.
Most hated, however, were the people who like them: the “flag-waving plastic-boater people”, he said. They are “kind of idiots because they support a power structure that keeps a foot on the throat of working-class people”.
Hmmm. “Power structure.” “The throat of working-class people.” What is this, 1867?
I must say, as an avowed lifelong anti-monarchist myself, I find it tiresome when I am lumped in with speaking-clock part-timers like Coogan, Jeremy “Donkey Jacket” Corbyn and the muppets from Republic, whose idea of a protest is off-the-peg Just Stop Oil-style stunting.
They just don’t get it.
If you truly want to get rid of the monarchy, it is a full-time job. You need to have covered every wedding; talked to the “flag-waving plastic-boater people”; waged a subtle but relentless war against ageing duchesses and minor royals (Zara Tindall was one of the most sullen people I’d ever interviewed).
You need to have scrutinised every measly podcast, livestream, shocking court case (not only Harry’s but Princess Anne’s, after her dogs attacked two children); pursed your lips at every useless soundbite, inadvisable glove/shoe/hat/tiara combo and haiku-like mouth-farting Palace release; and learnt every word they’ve made up (“dimensionality”).
You need to know what Diana called £50 notes (“pink grannies”) and what Paul Burrell shrieked when he was taken away after hiding Diana’s effects in his attic (“I want white lilies on my coffin”). You need to remember what Andrew called Fergie (a “fat cow”) and how many teddies he keeps in his room at Royal Lodge (72 — I didn’t even need to look that up).
You need to know what’s still in Andrew’s wardrobe (Fergie’s wedding dress) and what Anne said to a gun-wielding psycho when he told her to get out of her car (“Not bloody likely”). You need to be fully across how many holidays the Yorkies are capable of taking in a single 12-month period: 24.
Or how else will they be defeated? It simply isn’t enough to say on a pod that you’ve been into Waitrose and tried “King Charles’s ‘orange jiggers’” (it’s “a posh person’s name for just orange juice”, Coogan mewed). When fighting the Germans, what did Churchill do? He didn’t casually drawl platitudes about “kombucha” or “Tony Blair” to two other, less successful comedians in a Top Gear-style setting as per Off Menu. He didn’t answer the question: what is your “dream dessert”? (“Rhubarb.”) No: he studied the enemy obsessively.
And at least some of us know who the enemy is. Hot tip: it’s the royals themselves, not the poor, benighted “idiots” who support them. The “flag-wavers” Coogan so despises are the same 50 weirdos who turn up to everything. They’re mentally ill; monitored by the police. Coogan may be ready to fish for our sympathy after his difficulties with drugs and depression (“I thought I was going to die from taking cocaine”, ran one headline) but he’s short on it himself when it comes to people thinking or saying the wrong thing. Why kick down?
I think it’s revealing that he does: it tells us it is not the royals he hates most. The people he hates are those who won’t play working class according to his fake working-class agenda. Flag-wavers aren’t scum because they’re poorer and less educated than he is (the traditional reasons for hating the working classes); they’re scum because they don’t think the right thoughts. They don’t hate the royals as he does; they don’t lick Corbyn, jaunt into Waitrose, appear on podcasts, live in a picture-perfect village in one of Sussex’s celebrity belts. They don’t furlough their gardener and housekeeper.
They don’t have the luxury of picking and choosing pet causes while pretending they are “working-class” heroes. They don’t sign public attacks on Israel because it’s not risk-free for them. It’s not, as it is for Coogan, a mere brand-building exercise; an opportunity to hang out with all the other café society lightweights: the actresses, directors, Notting Hill models, designer-clad socialites and terminally confused transpersonal psychotherapists who turned up to the demonstrations in recent weeks (“#freepalestine is the new #fendibaguette,” sighs a friend). Coogan may have been working class long ago, but he isn’t now. In fact, looking at the way he talks about drugs, restaurants and posh orange juice, I’m having difficulty telling the difference between him and the average Etonian.
It’s funny, isn’t it, how British society was once organised with rich Etonians and Princess Beatrice at the top and comedians from Manchester at the bottom. Now Etonians and Angela Rayner’s Tory “scum” are despised beyond all recognition, while performative socialists like Coogan are allowed to do whatever they want, including play Savile on the BBC. If you want to know what he thinks of the little people, though, victims of Savile were invited to visit him in costume on set.
This grand delusion works for people like Corbyn and Coogan because it maintains their power at the expense of the people underneath. By telling us they act in the interests of “working-class people”, they can consolidate their control; they reap the benefits. He stays virtuous and rich; they stay poor. Win-win for him; big loss for the people he’s supposed to be fighting for.
So if you want to know who really has a “boot on the throat” of the working class, it’s people like him.
I see that Boris Johnson is hired at GB News: it’s a sensational coup for the channel.
Locked in what looked like a Farrow & Ball safe room in Stow-on-the-Wold, he told viewers on Friday he would be offering his “unvarnished views” on everything. “Russia, China, the war in Ukraine ...” he burbled.
The camera flicked back to the studio. “We got Boris done,” screamed the anchor, Patrick Christys.
Oh dear. Still, I’ll be watching, even though it blows my mind that a former prime minister is stooping to chatting with pundits and reading the news headlines on the pie-centric people’s channel. It’s fine for Farage and it’s fine for Rees-Mogg (ish — he can’t present), but isn’t this sort of scrounging work beneath Johnson? I wonder how far it will go. Reality TV? The channel’s answer to This Morning? Will Boris and Carrie become the new Dick and Angel from the French chateau, secretly overeating in the country and screaming four-letter words at producers? I feel we’ve already heard those tapes, though.
The problem with Johnson is that his thirst for validation far outstrips his abilities. He will continue serving himself up to bosses for big money, but it’s thin gruel he’s bringing in: no searing insights; predictable takes on everything. He lacks the lissom touch of serious television talent. You watch him like a toddler: in the hope he might say something truly silly. It’s a kind of television skill, but it’s not exactly David Frost, is it?

https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.subtitle: Campaigner set for court appearance next month
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greta-t.text:
Greta Thunberg has been charged with a public order offence after leading a protest outside a central London hotel hosting heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies.
The environmental activist is one of 26 people who were charged over a protest outside the InterContinental London hotel on Park Lane, which was hosting the annual Energy Intelligence Forum, an oil industry conference.
The alleged offences involved in the protest include obstructing the highway and failing to comply with a condition imposed under Section 14 of the Public Order Act.
Thunberg, 20, was led away from the hotel by Metropolitan Police officers, who arrested 29 people in total, and placed in the back of a marked van.
Protesters shouted “thank you Greta” as the activist was being searched.
The Metropolitan Police said Thunberg, whose address was given as Dorset, was charged with failing to comply with a condition imposed under Section 14 of the Public Order Act. She and other activists were bailed to appear at Westminster magistrates’ court on November 15.
The demonstration was organised by Fossil Fuel London and involved dozens of protesters blocking access to the hotel, with protesters holding banners, shouting “oily money out” and “cancel the conference”, while others lit yellow and pink smoke flares.
Activists from Greenpeace abseiled down from the roof of the hotel to unfurl a banner reading “Make big oil pay” during the demonstration.
The protesters claim that fossil fuel companies are deliberately slowing the global energy transition to renewables to make more profit.
A white fence surrounded the hotel entrance and kept protesters out of the hotel while police attempted to escort conference attendees through the crowd of chanting activists.
Fossil Fuel London said that Thunberg was among six protesters who were released from Wandsworth police station at 2am. The group said that some protesters were given bail conditions preventing them from entering Westminster until their court appearance in November.
Speakers at the annual event, which until 2019 was known as Oil & Money, included the chief executive of Saudi state oil giant Aramco and senior executives from BP.
Shell’s chief executive Wael Sawan had been due to attend the conference but instead appeared by videolink in light of the protests.
A spokeswoman for the Met said: “Officers responded to the protest on the morning of Tuesday, 17 October and imposed conditions to prevent disruption to the public. The protesters were asked to move from the road on to the pavement, which would enable them to continue with their demonstration without breaching the conditions. One woman, who was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage, has been bailed pending further enquiries”.
Usually, charges for failing to comply with section 14 of the Public Order Act are dealt with through a fine, although the maximum sentence is six months’ imprisonment.
Last week, a Swedish court found Thunberg guilty of disobeying a police order to leave a climate protest and fined her £335.

Greta Thunberg has been arrested by police after leading protests outside a central London hotel that was hosting the heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies.

Activists from Greenpeace abseiled from the roof of the hotel to unfurl a banner reading “make big oil pay”.
A white fence surrounded the hotel entrance and kept protesters out while police attempted to escort conference attendees through the crowd of chanting activists.
The protesters claim that fossil fuel companies are deliberately slowing the global energy transition to renewables in order to make more profit.
Nuri Syed Corser, of Fossil Free London, said: “We need direct action to take back the power from the oil elite that has gathered here today behind closed doors. Their only plan is to profit at our expense. Arrests like these will not deter us. Our right to protest is our own, it is not given to us by the government.”
Addressing reporters before her arrest, Thunberg said: “The world is drowning in fossil fuels. Our hopes and dreams and lives are being washed away by a flood of greenwashing and lies.
“It has been clear for decades that the fossil fuel industries were well aware of the consequences of their business models, and yet, they have done nothing.
“The opposite – they have actively delayed, distracted and denied the causes of the climate crisis and spread doubts about their own engagement in it.”
Thunberg added: “We cannot let this continue. The elite of the oil and money conference, they have no intention of transition.
“Their plan is to continue this destructive search of profits. That is why we have to take direct action to stop this and to kick oil money out of politics.
“We have no other option but to put our bodies outside this conference and to physically disrupt. And we have to do that every time, we have to continue showing them that they are not going to get away with this.”
Maja Darlington, a campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said: “Big oil is profiting from humanity’s loss and those who have done the least to cause climate change are being forced to pay the price.”
The Met said officers had “continued discussions with the protesters” and made “interventions” to enable members of the public safe access in and out of the venue.
“Officers on scene have kept this under constant review and at 12.32pm imposed conditions on the group under section 14 of the Public Order Act given to prevent serious disruption to the community, hotel and guests,” he said.
“Officers asked the protesters to move from the road onto the pavement, which would enable them to continue with their demonstration without breaching the conditions. A number of protesters failed to do so and we have now made a further 14 arrests for section 14 of the Public Order Act and a further one for criminal damage. Officers remain on scene.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.title: Labour fury at security lapses over Keir Starmer glitter protester
https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.subtitle: Read our photographer’s verdict at the end
https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.text:
Labour is urgently reviewing security arrangements after a protester was able to storm the party’s conference stage and pour glitter over Sir Keir Starmer.
Yaz Ashmawi, 28, a physicist turned Extinction Rebellion strategist, was arrested after he threw glitter over Starmer as he prepared to give his keynote speech.
• The key points and policies from Starmer’s speech and Labour conference
Ashmawi, who was representing the group People Demand Democracy and was wearing a T-shirt bearing its name, ran from the back of the hall to Starmer’s podium.
The Labour leader pushed Ashmawi — whose full name is Yasine El-Ashmawi — away from the microphone as the protester grabbed Starmer’s shoulder and wrist.
It took more than ten seconds for security staff to reach the pair. When they did, he was dropped to the floor and dragged away shouting, as Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, angrily said: “For god’s sake.”
Starmer has described the protester as an “idiot” and said he was “absolutely determined” to ignore him.
He told Times Radio on Wednesday: “I was absolutely determined that this wasn’t going to disrupt what has been four years of really hard work, getting the Labour Party from where we landed in 2019, which is a very bad place to this last conference before the general election, where we had to set out and did set out our positive case.”
He said he viewed the speech as a “culminating” moment. “I’ve always seen this as three stages. I took over three and a half years ago, picked it up off the floor. We had to change the party, expose the Tories and SNP as not fit to govern, then setting out the positive case, making the case that this doesn’t have to be another decade of decline.”
Starmer added: “I was determined we would get on with it. I just wanted to get on with the speech, and that’s why I rolled up my sleeves and got on with it. I didn’t want that idiot to interrupt that.”
Angela Rayner, the party’s deputy leader, said on Tuesday that she had “never seen Rachel Reeves so angry” and told LBC: “I thought I was going to do a full John Prescott at one point.”
Prescott, as deputy prime minister in 2001, punched a protester who egged him during a pro-hunting rally in Rhyl.
A Labour source said that they were “really f***ing angry” over the slow response, adding: “If he had a weapon, Keir could’ve been killed.”
A senior party source blamed the Metropolitan Police, since Starmer has round-the-clock protection. The Times understands that Met officers were in the hall during his speech as well as security staff provided by the venue, ACC Liverpool.
The Met said that it did not comment on security matters. ACC Liverpool said that “highly trained stewarding and security teams ensured the incident was dealt with appropriately”.
People Demand Democracy has been linked to Just Stop Oil and is calling for a proportional voting system for elections and a “House of Citizens” to replace the House of Lords, selected by “democratic lottery”. A Just Stop Oil insider described the group, which was set up this year, as a “coalition member”.
A representative for People Demand Democracy, who gave her name as Aria, told Times Radio: “We’re rooted in non-violence so the action was designed not to cause harm.”
However, another Labour source said: “Security didn’t work today, for whatever reason, and that’s what we’ll be reviewing with urgency.”
Graham Wettone, a former Metropolitan Police officer, said: “Anyone who gets that close is clearly a breach in security. The risk and danger depends on a number of things. Clearly, there has been a breach of security.
“But you can’t have security standing right alongside Starmer and his protection officers acted quite quickly. It comes down to how closely you want your security. It depends on what your principal wants from you, balanced with an assessment of the threat.
“The action from the cops looks fairly reasonable to me and they dealt with him quickly and reasonably. But it’s a breach of the venue’s security and questions must be asked about how the protester was able to get onto the stage.”
Those attending the conference have to have a conference pass, issued after an accreditation process, and any bags have to be scanned or searched. The security arrangements are relatively light compared with the airport-style scanners in place at the Conservative Party conference in Manchester.
A Labour spokesman said that Starmer was “fine” and “completely unfazed”. While cameras broadcasting the speech were cut as the incident unfolded, Starmer remained on stage while the man was removed. Carol Linforth, a veteran Labour staff member and the party’s director of events, helped Starmer to remove his jacket.
Starmer told members, who got to their feet to cheer and applaud: “If he thinks that bothers me, he doesn’t know me. Protest or power, that’s why we’ve changed our party, conference.”
After the speech Yvette Cooper, the shadow home secretary, said that Labour was a “party of power, not protest”. She told BBC News: “It just shows, doesn’t it, that you can’t bother Keir Starmer with stuff like that. It’s about power not protest, that is what Keir Starmer was talking about. We’re a party of power not protest.”
Last month, People Demand Democracy gave Starmer and Rishi Sunak an ultimatum to implement its demands by September 30 or face “proportionate action”.
Ashmawi, who goes by the alias “Dove”, is from Surrey and holds two master’s degrees in theoretical physics, one from the University of St Andrews and the other from the University of Cambridge.
He attended primary school in Oxted, Surrey, before moving to Dubai and studying at Dubai College, one of the Middle East’s leading private schools which charges more than £24,000 a year.
After working as a web designer, videographer and photographer, he joined Extinction Rebellion full-time as a member of the group’s strategy team.
He has previously been at the forefront of XR’s protests and in one case led protesters in a march along the River Clyde in Glasgow during Cop 26. This year he told Yahoo News UK that XR had changed and that it was “not just blocking random junctions any more” and instead “coming to the centre of power”.
The ACC Liverpool group, which runs the venue where Labour is holding its annual conference, said it “recognises the rights of all groups and individuals to free speech and freedom of expression” but said the safety of its speakers and customers was of the “utmost importance”.
Shabana Mahmood, the shadow justice minister, told BBC Radio 4’s PM programme: “I’m sure questions are being asked. We will want to make sure that nothing like that can ever happen again.”
A spokesman for Merseyside police said that Ashmawi had been arrested on suspicion of a section 39 assault, breach of the peace and causing public nuisance, and would be questioned.
At 1.20pm, everything was going to plan for Labour’s PR machine (James Glossop, Times photographer, writes). A crowd of jolly placard-wielding activists was assembled to cheer as Sir Keir Starmer and his wife Victoria walked towards a dozen or so photographers and a TV crew. This was the early picture, provided to use before the speech begins to satisfy any publications with early deadlines. It also takes place in somewhere with a bit of natural light, not something that is in abundance at party conferences.
Forty-five minutes later, things were no longer going to plan. A protester strode on to the stage in Liverpool before Starmer had even started his speech, and threw glitter all over him. This is the kind of thing we photographers need to be ready for. Although the protester’s message wasn’t particularly clear and the subsequent reporting of the speech mentioned the incident only as a side-note, I would bet that it will be the main image from the speech used in most newspapers on Wednesday morning.
Shooting a political speech is all about reading the mood of the room, weighing up where the good backgrounds are and paying attention. The most important moments to pay attention are during the first five minutes and the last five minutes. This is when ordinarily wooden politicians may start getting animated and waving to no one in particular, hugging their colleagues, gesturing to the crowd, that kind of thing. Which all make better pictures than a talking head. Had the protest happened in the middle of the speech, it may have been missed by quite a few photographers.
I decided to shoot from the back of the room, on a TV platform I probably wasn’t supposed to be on, using my 100-400mm lens at 400mm. The platform allows enough height to get clear of the audience when they stand to applaud at the beginning. It’s normally sensible to keep “on” the speaker until the cadence of their speech shifts into a more regular rhythm, and they start moving through each of the many topics they feel obliged to cover.
After this had happened there really was no point in shooting any of the standard “man points while looking serious” type pictures, so I rushed back to the laptop to file the glitter images before the paper’s important afternoon meeting, also called “conference”. One of the set held the front of our website for several hours.
I was wondering after the event if the police or party security would be in trouble for not reacting quickly enough. Starmer’s reaction in the sequence of images shows what I read to be a certain amount of disbelief at what was happening, or at least that it took seemingly so long for someone to intervene. Labour are odds on by quite a margin to win the next election. Whether they win or not, my guess is that security will be quite a bit tighter at next year’s conference.
